A query for read every user name and city is SELECT name, city FROM users;. Only the required columns are returned, which is clearer than SELECT *.
To read user id, name, and status, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, status FROM users;. The column list after SELECT determines which fields appear in the result.
In one common scenario, list all product names and prices can be written as SELECT name, price FROM products;. FROM identifies products as the source table.
One way to list product id, name, and stock is SELECT id, name, stock FROM products;. This is a read-only operation and does not modify product data.
An SQL statement for read order id, user id, and amount is SELECT id, user_id, amount FROM orders;. Explicit columns avoid returning unrelated fields.
A query for read order status and creation time is SELECT id, status, created_at FROM orders;. A SELECT statement can return several fields at once.
To list employee names and salaries, one SQL form is SELECT name, salary FROM employees;. Without WHERE, all employee rows are eligible to be returned.
In one common scenario, list employee id, name, and hire date can be written as SELECT id, name, hire_date FROM employees;. The field order also determines the column order in the result.
One way to list student names and cities is SELECT name, city FROM students;. This projects two columns without filtering rows.
An SQL statement for read student id, subject, and score is SELECT student_id, subject, score FROM scores;. Each result row still corresponds to one score record.
A query for list article titles and status is SELECT title, status FROM articles;. This is useful when a list page needs only a few display fields.
To read article id, title, and publication time, one SQL form is SELECT id, title, published_at FROM articles;. Rows with NULL published_at still appear because no filter is applied.
In one common scenario, read each comment article id and content can be written as SELECT article_id, content FROM comments;. SELECT chooses columns; it does not filter rows.
One way to read comment id, user id, and creation time is SELECT id, user_id, created_at FROM comments;. Add WHERE when the rows themselves need to be filtered.
An SQL statement for list all department ids and names is SELECT id, name FROM departments;. Even for a small table, explicit columns make intent clearer.
A query for return only user names is SELECT name FROM users;. A single-column SELECT returns only name.
To read the category from every product, one SQL form is SELECT category FROM products;. Duplicates are preserved; use DISTINCT for unique categories.
In one common scenario, read the amount from every order can be written as SELECT amount FROM orders;. SELECT amount does not calculate a total; use SUM for that.
One way to read every employee department id is SELECT department_id FROM employees;. Several employees may share the same department id, so duplicates are possible.
An SQL statement for read the subject from every score row is SELECT subject FROM scores;. Use SELECT DISTINCT subject when a unique subject list is required.
A query for find users who are at least 18 is SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age >= 18;. WHERE removes rows that do not satisfy the condition.
To find users in beijing, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE city = 'Beijing';. String literals are normally written in single quotes.
In one common scenario, find active users can be written as SELECT name, status FROM users WHERE status = 'active';. Equality performs an exact match on the status value.
One way to find products priced below 100 is SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price < 100;. Numeric fields can be filtered with comparison operators.
An SQL statement for find products with zero stock is SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE stock = 0;. This kind of condition is commonly used to find out-of-stock items.
A query for find orders with amount at least 500 is SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 500;. Only orders meeting the amount threshold are returned.
To find orders that are not cancelled, one SQL form is SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled';. <> is the standard not-equal operator.
In one common scenario, find employees earning above 10000 can be written as SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 10000;. WHERE operates on individual employee rows.
One way to find employees hired in 2025 or later is SELECT name, hire_date FROM employees WHERE hire_date >= DATE '2025-01-01';. The DATE literal makes the date comparison explicit.
An SQL statement for find students in beijing or shanghai is SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE city IN ('Beijing', 'Shanghai');. IN is convenient for matching one of several values.
A query for find math scores of at least 90 is SELECT student_id, score FROM scores WHERE subject = 'math' AND score >= 90;. AND requires both conditions to be true.
To find scores between 80 and 89, one SQL form is SELECT student_id, subject, score FROM scores WHERE score BETWEEN 80 AND 89;. BETWEEN includes both boundaries here.
In one common scenario, find published articles can be written as SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE status = 'published';. WHERE can filter an enumerated status field.
One way to find articles published since 2026 is SELECT title, published_at FROM articles WHERE published_at >= DATE '2026-01-01';. Date range filtering normally belongs in WHERE.
An SQL statement for find comments containing sql is SELECT id, content FROM comments WHERE content LIKE '%SQL%';. LIKE with percent signs performs simple pattern matching.
A query for find users with a known age is SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age IS NOT NULL;. NULL checks use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
To find orders with no associated user id, one SQL form is SELECT id, user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NULL;. IS NULL tests for missing values.

In one common scenario, find products outside electronics can be written as SELECT name, category FROM products WHERE category <> 'electronics';. Rows with NULL category do not automatically satisfy the not-equal comparison.
One way to find employees in departments 1, 2, or 3 is SELECT name, department_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (1, 2, 3);. IN is more compact than repeating several OR conditions.
An SQL statement for find users whose names start with a is SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'A%';. A% matches text starting with A followed by any characters.
A query for list users from oldest to youngest is SELECT id, name, age FROM users ORDER BY age DESC;. DESC means descending order.
To list users from newest to oldest signup, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, created_at FROM users ORDER BY created_at DESC;. Descending time order places the newest records first.
In one common scenario, list products from lowest to highest price can be written as SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price ASC;. ASC means ascending order.
One way to list products from highest to lowest stock is SELECT name, stock FROM products ORDER BY stock DESC;. ORDER BY changes order without filtering rows.
An SQL statement for sort orders from highest to lowest amount is SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC;. Larger order amounts appear first.
A query for sort orders from oldest to newest is SELECT id, created_at FROM orders ORDER BY created_at ASC;. This is useful for chronological review.
To sort employees by salary descending, one SQL form is SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;. Without a secondary key, ties may have unspecified order.

In one common scenario, sort by salary descending and hire date ascending can be written as SELECT name, salary, hire_date FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, hire_date ASC;. Multiple sort keys are applied from left to right.
One way to sort students by city and then name is SELECT name, city FROM students ORDER BY city ASC, name ASC;. The second key orders rows tied on the first.
An SQL statement for sort scores from highest to lowest is SELECT student_id, subject, score FROM scores ORDER BY score DESC;. Higher scores appear first.
A query for list articles by publication time descending is SELECT title, published_at FROM articles ORDER BY published_at DESC;. The position of NULL values can depend on database rules.
To list comments from newest to oldest, one SQL form is SELECT id, created_at FROM comments ORDER BY created_at DESC;. This is a common activity-feed ordering.
In one common scenario, sort departments alphabetically can be written as SELECT id, name FROM departments ORDER BY name ASC;. Text fields can also be sort keys.
One way to sort products by category then price descending is SELECT name, category, price FROM products ORDER BY category ASC, price DESC;. One ORDER BY can combine multiple fields.
An SQL statement for sort by age descending and name ascending for ties is SELECT name, age FROM users ORDER BY age DESC, name ASC;. A secondary key makes tied output more deterministic.
A query for sort orders by status then amount descending is SELECT id, status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY status ASC, amount DESC;. Text and numeric fields can be combined in ordering.
To sort by subject then score descending, one SQL form is SELECT student_id, subject, score FROM scores ORDER BY subject ASC, score DESC;. This is useful for viewing scores within each subject.
In one common scenario, sort articles by id descending can be written as SELECT id, title FROM articles ORDER BY id DESC;. Increasing ids may resemble recency, but real timestamps are safer.
One way to sort user names in descending lexical order is SELECT id, name FROM users ORDER BY name DESC;. Text ordering is also affected by collation rules.

An SQL statement for sort by price descending and id ascending for ties is SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC;. A deterministic tie breaker is especially helpful for pagination.
A query for count orders for each status is SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY status;. Rows are grouped by status and COUNT counts each group.
To calculate total order amount per user, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;. SUM adds amount values inside each user group.

In one common scenario, calculate average order amount per user can be written as SELECT user_id, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;. AVG calculates a mean within each user group.
One way to count products in each category is SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category;. Each category produces one aggregate row.
An SQL statement for calculate average price by category is SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products GROUP BY category;. The non-aggregate category column appears in GROUP BY.
A query for calculate total stock by category is SELECT category, SUM(stock) AS total_stock FROM products GROUP BY category;. SUM totals stock inside each category.
To count employees in each department, one SQL form is SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;. Rows are grouped by department_id before counting.

In one common scenario, calculate average salary by department can be written as SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;. AVG ignores NULL salary values.
One way to calculate salary total by department is SELECT department_id, SUM(salary) AS total_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;. This summarizes salary scale by department.
An SQL statement for calculate average score per subject is SELECT subject, AVG(score) AS avg_score FROM scores GROUP BY subject;. Each subject becomes one group.
A query for count score rows per subject is SELECT subject, COUNT(*) AS score_count FROM scores GROUP BY subject;. COUNT(*) counts rows in each group.
To calculate each student average score, one SQL form is SELECT student_id, AVG(score) AS avg_score FROM scores GROUP BY student_id;. Multiple subject rows are aggregated by student id.
In one common scenario, count articles by status can be written as SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS article_count FROM articles GROUP BY status;. GROUP BY is useful for status-distribution reports.
One way to count comments for each article is SELECT article_id, COUNT(*) AS comment_count FROM comments GROUP BY article_id;. Only article ids appearing in comments are represented.
An SQL statement for count users by city is SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM users GROUP BY city;. Users with the same city are placed in one group.
A query for count users by status is SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM users GROUP BY status;. Aggregate results are useful for reporting summaries.
To calculate total amount by order status, one SQL form is SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY status;. Amounts are summed inside each status group.
In one common scenario, find minimum price in each category can be written as SELECT category, MIN(price) AS min_price FROM products GROUP BY category;. MIN can be used with GROUP BY.
One way to find maximum price in each category is SELECT category, MAX(price) AS max_price FROM products GROUP BY category;. Each category returns one maximum value.

An SQL statement for find minimum and maximum salary per department is SELECT department_id, MIN(salary) AS min_salary, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;. Several aggregate functions can be used in one grouped query.
A query for show user names with order ids and amounts is SELECT u. id AS order_id, o. amount FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON u. user_id;. INNER JOIN returns only matching users and orders.
To show users with their order status, one SQL form is SELECT u. status FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON u. user_id;. A user with several orders can appear on several rows.

In one common scenario, show department names with employee names can be written as SELECT d. name AS department_name, e. name AS employee_name FROM departments d INNER JOIN employees e ON d. department_id;. The primary and foreign keys connect the tables.

One way to show student names with subject scores is SELECT s. name, sc. subject, sc. score FROM students s INNER JOIN scores sc ON s. student_id;. JOIN combines student identity data with score facts.
An SQL statement for show article titles with comments is SELECT a. content FROM articles a INNER JOIN comments c ON a. article_id;. Only articles with matching comments appear in an INNER JOIN.
A query for show author names with article titles is SELECT u. name AS author_name, a. title FROM users u INNER JOIN articles a ON u. author_id;. author_id connects each article to a user.
To show commenter names with content, one SQL form is SELECT u. content FROM users u INNER JOIN comments c ON u. user_id;. This avoids duplicating user names in the comments table.
In one common scenario, show order id, user name, and amount can be written as SELECT o. amount FROM orders o INNER JOIN users u ON o. Join conditions should use stable keys rather than names.
One way to show employees with department names is SELECT e. name AS department_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e. Table aliases make column ownership clearer.
An SQL statement for show comment ids with article titles is SELECT c. title FROM comments c INNER JOIN articles a ON c. Each comment points to an article through article_id.
A query for show scores with student names is SELECT sc. subject, sc. name FROM scores sc INNER JOIN students s ON sc. JOIN can reconstruct a business view from normalized tables.
To show article titles with authors, one SQL form is SELECT a. name AS author FROM articles a INNER JOIN users u ON a. The article author foreign key references users. id.

In one common scenario, show users and order creation times can be written as SELECT u. created_at FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON u. user_id;. JOIN does not automatically deduplicate one-to-many relationships.
One way to show departments with employee salaries is SELECT d. salary FROM departments d INNER JOIN employees e ON d. department_id;. Each matching employee creates one joined row.
An SQL statement for show students with score values is SELECT s. name, sc. score FROM students s INNER JOIN scores sc ON s. student_id;. Several subject scores can create several rows per student.
A query for show authors with article status is SELECT u. status FROM users u INNER JOIN articles a ON u. author_id;. INNER JOIN excludes users with no articles.
To show articles with commenter user ids, one SQL form is SELECT a. user_id FROM articles a INNER JOIN comments c ON a. article_id;. Commenter details could be added with another JOIN to users.
In one common scenario, show order status with user city can be written as SELECT o. city FROM orders o INNER JOIN users u ON o. A multi-table query can combine fields from different entities.
One way to show employees and department ids is SELECT e. id AS department_id FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e. Aliases can avoid ambiguity when tables share column names.
An SQL statement for show comments, commenter names, and times is SELECT c. created_at FROM comments c INNER JOIN users u ON c. JOIN turns a foreign key into readable related information.
To count all orders, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders;. COUNT(*) counts rows in the result.
To calculate total order amount, one SQL form is SELECT SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM orders;. SUM adds non-NULL amount values.
To calculate average order amount, one SQL form is SELECT AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders;. AVG returns the mean of non-NULL amount values.
To count all products, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products;. Without GROUP BY, the whole table is one aggregate scope.
To calculate average product price, one SQL form is SELECT AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products;. The result normally contains one row.
To calculate total product stock, one SQL form is SELECT SUM(stock) AS total_stock FROM products;. SUM is appropriate for additive numeric values.
To count all employees, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees;. COUNT(*) does not require choosing a non-NULL column.
To calculate average salary, one SQL form is SELECT AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees;. AVG ignores NULL salary values.
To calculate total salary, one SQL form is SELECT SUM(salary) AS total_salary FROM employees;. If all salary values are NULL, SUM commonly returns NULL.
To count all users, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM users;. This is a basic row-count pattern.
To count users with known age, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(age) AS known_age_count FROM users;. COUNT(age) does not count rows where age is NULL.
To calculate average score, one SQL form is SELECT AVG(score) AS avg_score FROM scores;. This is one average across all score rows.
To count score records, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS score_count FROM scores;. It counts rows, not distinct students.
To count all comments, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS comment_count FROM comments;. Use COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) for distinct commenters.
To count all articles, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(*) AS article_count FROM articles;. Aggregate queries can directly produce reporting metrics.
To count distinct buyers, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS buyer_count FROM orders;. DISTINCT inside COUNT counts unique user ids.
To find minimum product price, one SQL form is SELECT MIN(price) AS min_price FROM products;. MIN returns the smallest non-NULL value.
To find maximum product price, one SQL form is SELECT MAX(price) AS max_price FROM products;. MAX returns the largest non-NULL value.
To find minimum and maximum order amounts, one SQL form is SELECT MIN(amount) AS min_amount, MAX(amount) AS max_amount FROM orders;. Several aggregate functions can appear in one SELECT.
To find earliest hire date, one SQL form is SELECT MIN(hire_date) AS earliest_hire FROM employees;. MIN can also be applied to sortable dates.

To find orders above the average amount, one SQL form is SELECT id, user_id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders);. The subquery computes the average first and the outer query filters with it.
To find products above the average price, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);. The scalar subquery returns one average value.
To find employees above company average salary, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);. This is a typical scalar-subquery use case.
To find users who placed an order, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL);. The inner query produces a user-id set used by IN.

To find users who never placed an order, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o. id);. NOT EXISTS naturally expresses the absence of related rows.
To find articles with at least one comment, one SQL form is SELECT id, title FROM articles a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM comments c WHERE c. id);. EXISTS only checks whether a matching row exists.

To find articles with no comments, one SQL form is SELECT id, title FROM articles a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM comments c WHERE c. id);. The inner query references the outer article id, making it correlated.

To find employees above their department average, one SQL form is SELECT e. salary FROM employees e WHERE e. salary > (SELECT AVG(e2. salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2. department_id);. Each employee is compared with the average salary of that employee department.

To find scores above the average for the same subject, one SQL form is SELECT s1. student_id, s1. subject, s1. score FROM scores s1 WHERE s1. score > (SELECT AVG(s2. score) FROM scores s2 WHERE s2. subject = s1. subject);. This correlated subquery computes a benchmark for the current subject.

To find products below average stock, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, stock FROM products WHERE stock < (SELECT AVG(stock) FROM products);. The subquery result becomes the comparison value in the outer WHERE.

To find departments that have employees, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM departments WHERE id IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL);. An IN subquery is useful for obtaining candidate keys from another table.

To find departments with no employees, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM departments d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e. id);. NOT EXISTS expresses that no related employee exists.

To find the order or orders with maximum amount, one SQL form is SELECT id, user_id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM orders);. If several orders tie for the maximum, all are returned.

To find the cheapest product or products, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price = (SELECT MIN(price) FROM products);. The subquery gets the minimum price and the outer query returns all ties.

To find users created before the earliest order, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, created_at FROM users WHERE created_at < (SELECT MIN(created_at) FROM orders);. A scalar aggregate subquery can bring a summary value from another table.

To find students with at least one score below 60, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM scores sc WHERE sc. id AND sc. score < 60);. EXISTS becomes true as soon as a matching low-score row exists.

To find students with no score below 60, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM scores sc WHERE sc. id AND sc. score < 60);. The rule is expressed as the absence of any low score.

To find products above the electronics average price, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products WHERE category = 'electronics');. The inner WHERE restricts which products contribute to the average.

To find authors whose article count is above the average author count, one SQL form is SELECT author_id, COUNT(*) AS article_count FROM articles GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM articles GROUP BY author_id) x);. The inner query computes counts per author and then their average.

To find commented articles whose comment count is above the average, one SQL form is SELECT article_id, COUNT(*) AS comment_count FROM comments GROUP BY article_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM comments GROUP BY article_id) x);. HAVING compares each article aggregated comment count.

To find users with more than 5 orders, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;. A common mistake is WHERE COUNT(*) > 5. WHERE filters detail rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregate groups afterward.

To find users whose average order amount exceeds 300, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING AVG(amount) > 300;. AVG(amount) is a group-level value, so the condition belongs in HAVING.

To filter paid orders first, then find users whose total exceeds 1000, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY user_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000;. WHERE filters raw orders first and HAVING filters the user totals afterward.

To find departments with average salary above 15000, one SQL form is SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 15000;. Average salary is an aggregate value and should be filtered with HAVING.

To exclude employees with no department, then find departments with at least 10 employees, one SQL form is SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;. WHERE handles raw NULL rows and HAVING evaluates the group count.

To find subjects with average score at least 85, one SQL form is SELECT subject, AVG(score) AS avg_score FROM scores GROUP BY subject HAVING AVG(score) >= 85;. WHERE AVG(score) >= 85 cannot filter an aggregate at the same query level.

To consider passing scores only, then find subjects with more than 20 passing rows, one SQL form is SELECT subject, COUNT(*) AS pass_count FROM scores WHERE score >= 60 GROUP BY subject HAVING COUNT(*) > 20;. This demonstrates WHERE for detail rows and HAVING for grouped results.

To find categories with more than 50 products, one SQL form is SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 50;. COUNT(*) > 50 describes a whole category rather than an individual product.

To filter positive-priced products, then find categories with average price below 100, one SQL form is SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products WHERE price > 0 GROUP BY category HAVING AVG(price) < 100;. The raw price condition belongs in WHERE; the category average belongs in HAVING.

To find articles with at least 10 comments, one SQL form is SELECT article_id, COUNT(*) AS comment_count FROM comments GROUP BY article_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;. The comment-count threshold is applied after aggregation.

To find categories with total stock above 1000, one SQL form is SELECT category, SUM(stock) AS total_stock FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING SUM(stock) > 1000;. SUM(stock) is a group-level result.

To find departments whose maximum salary exceeds 30000, one SQL form is SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING MAX(salary) > 30000;. MAX(salary) should be filtered by HAVING.

To consider active users only, then find cities with over 100 users, one SQL form is SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS active_users FROM users WHERE status = 'active' GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;. status is a row condition, while the city count is a group condition.

To find users whose total order amount is zero, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING SUM(amount) = 0;. The total amount is an aggregate result.

To find students whose minimum score is at least 60, one SQL form is SELECT student_id, MIN(score) AS min_score FROM scores GROUP BY student_id HAVING MIN(score) >= 60;. Using WHERE score >= 60 would remove low scores before aggregation and change the question.
To find categories with average stock below 10, one SQL form is SELECT category, AVG(stock) AS avg_stock FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING AVG(stock) < 10;. Average stock is an aggregate value.

To consider 2026 orders only, then find users with more than 20 orders, one SQL form is SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE created_at >= DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 20;. The time filter occurs before grouping and the count threshold afterward.

To find authors with at least 5 articles, one SQL form is SELECT author_id, COUNT(*) AS article_count FROM articles GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;. Author article counts must be aggregated before filtering.

To filter published articles first, then find authors with at least 3, one SQL form is SELECT author_id, COUNT(*) AS published_count FROM articles WHERE status = 'published' GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;. WHERE controls which articles enter the count; HAVING controls which author groups remain.

To find order statuses with more than 50 distinct buyers, one SQL form is SELECT status, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS buyer_count FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) > 50;. The distinct-buyer count is still a group-level aggregate result.

To show all users and any orders they may have, one SQL form is SELECT u. id AS order_id, o. amount FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. LEFT JOIN preserves every user. Users with no orders have NULL order fields, while INNER JOIN would exclude them.

To show all articles and any comments they may have, one SQL form is SELECT a. id AS comment_id, c. content FROM articles a LEFT JOIN comments c ON c. LEFT JOIN is appropriate when zero-comment articles must remain.

To show all departments and any employees they may have, one SQL form is SELECT d. name AS employee_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e. Departments without employees still appear with NULL employee fields.

To count orders for every user, including zero-order users, one SQL form is SELECT u. name, COUNT(o. id) AS order_count FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. id GROUP BY u. name;. COUNT(o. id) is important; COUNT(*) would count the placeholder row created by LEFT JOIN.

To count comments for every article, including zero-comment articles, one SQL form is SELECT a. title, COUNT(c. id) AS comment_count FROM articles a LEFT JOIN comments c ON c. id GROUP BY a. title;. LEFT JOIN preserves all articles while COUNT(c. id) counts only real comments.

To show average salary for all departments, including empty departments, one SQL form is SELECT d. name, AVG(e. salary) AS avg_salary FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e. id GROUP BY d. name;. An empty department gets a NULL average rather than automatically becoming zero.

To show only users that actually have orders, one SQL form is SELECT u. id AS order_id FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON o. Because a matching order is required, INNER JOIN is the appropriate choice.
To show only articles that have comments, one SQL form is SELECT a. id AS comment_id FROM articles a INNER JOIN comments c ON c. INNER JOIN keeps only matching article-comment pairs.

To show all employees and department names when available, one SQL form is SELECT e. name AS department_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d. department_id;. Putting employees on the left preserves every employee.

To show all students and any score rows they may have, one SQL form is SELECT s. name, sc. subject, sc. score FROM students s LEFT JOIN scores sc ON sc. Students with no scores remain with NULL score fields.

To find users with no orders, one SQL form is SELECT u. name FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. id WHERE o. id IS NULL;. After LEFT JOIN, unmatched right-side ids are NULL and can identify missing relationships.
To find articles with no comments, one SQL form is SELECT a. title FROM articles a LEFT JOIN comments c ON c. id WHERE c. id IS NULL;. This is a common LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL anti-join pattern.

To find departments with no employees, one SQL form is SELECT d. name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e. id WHERE e. id IS NULL;. With INNER JOIN, empty departments would disappear before filtering.

To show total order amount for every user, using zero for users with no orders, one SQL form is SELECT u. name, COALESCE(SUM(o. amount), 0) AS total_amount FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. id GROUP BY u. name;. LEFT JOIN preserves users and COALESCE converts a NULL total to zero.

To count employees in every department, including empty departments, one SQL form is SELECT d. name, COUNT(e. id) AS employee_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e. id GROUP BY d. name;. LEFT JOIN with COUNT(e. id) correctly gives zero for empty departments.

To show only students with at least one score row, one SQL form is SELECT DISTINCT s. name FROM students s INNER JOIN scores sc ON sc. INNER JOIN excludes students with no scores, and DISTINCT removes duplicates from multiple subjects.
To show all users as potential authors and any articles they have, one SQL form is SELECT u. title FROM users u LEFT JOIN articles a ON a. Use LEFT JOIN when users with no articles must still appear.
To show all orders and user names when available, one SQL form is SELECT o. name FROM orders o LEFT JOIN users u ON u. user_id;. Placing orders on the left preserves every order row.

To compare inner join and left join for users and orders, one SQL form is SELECT u. id AS order_id FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. Changing to INNER JOIN would keep only users with orders; LEFT JOIN keeps every user.

To find employee rows that have a matching department, one SQL form is SELECT e. name AS department_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON d. department_id;. Because a matching department is required, INNER JOIN is more direct.
To find users whose age is unknown, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE age IS NULL;. Do not use age = NULL. NULL represents unknown, so ordinary equality does not evaluate to TRUE.
To find users whose age is known, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, age FROM users WHERE age IS NOT NULL;. Use IS NOT NULL to test for a known value.
To find articles with no publication time, one SQL form is SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE published_at IS NULL;. NULL commonly represents a value that has not been set.

To find published articles that also have a publication time, one SQL form is SELECT id, title, published_at FROM articles WHERE status = 'published' AND published_at IS NOT NULL;. A status condition and NULL check can be combined with AND.

To display unknown when a user city is null, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city FROM users;. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument and can provide a display fallback.

To display zero when product stock is null, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, COALESCE(stock, 0) AS stock FROM products;. This is a display fallback and does not make stored NULL semantically identical to a real zero.
To count users with a non-null age, one SQL form is SELECT COUNT(age) AS known_age_count FROM users;. COUNT(age) ignores NULL values, while COUNT(*) counts every row.
To calculate average salary with null semantics, one SQL form is SELECT AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees;. AVG ignores NULL salary values rather than treating them as zero.
To find employees with no department id, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NULL;. IS NULL is the standard missing-value check.
To find orders with an associated user id, one SQL form is SELECT id, user_id, amount FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL;. This excludes orders whose user_id is missing.

To find users outside beijing while excluding unknown cities, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, city FROM users WHERE city <> 'Beijing' AND city IS NOT NULL;. NULL is not treated as simply not equal to Beijing by an ordinary comparison.
To find users in beijing or with an unknown city, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, city FROM users WHERE city = 'Beijing' OR city IS NULL;. NULL requires an explicit IS NULL condition.

To count comments for every article including zero, one SQL form is SELECT a. title, COUNT(c. id) AS comment_count FROM articles a LEFT JOIN comments c ON c. id GROUP BY a. title;. COUNT(c. id) ignores NULL, so an article with no comments gets zero.

To show zero total amount for users with no orders, one SQL form is SELECT u. name, COALESCE(SUM(o. amount), 0) AS total_amount FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o. id GROUP BY u. name;. SUM may be NULL when no amounts exist, and COALESCE converts that to zero.

To identify users whose city is empty string rather than null, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE city = '';. An empty string is a known text value, while NULL represents missing or unknown information.
To find users whose city is neither null nor empty, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, city FROM users WHERE city IS NOT NULL AND city <> '';. NULL and empty strings need separate checks.

To use a fallback date when published_at is null for sorting, one SQL form is SELECT id, title, published_at FROM articles ORDER BY COALESCE(published_at, DATE '1900-01-01') DESC;. COALESCE can provide a replacement value for NULL inside an ordering expression.
To find products whose stock is unknown rather than zero, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE stock IS NULL;. stock IS NULL means unknown stock; stock = 0 means a known zero quantity.

To find employees with known salary above 10000, one SQL form is SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL AND salary > 10000;. The explicit IS NOT NULL makes the business meaning clear.

To avoid a null-related not in trap, one SQL form is SELECT id, name FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o. id);. If a subquery can contain NULL, NOT IN may behave unexpectedly under three-valued logic; NOT EXISTS is often safer for missing relationships.

In practice, choosing sorting, search, and graph algorithms requires complexity reasoning to judge scalability. It also helps to distinguish it from nearby ideas: time complexity describes computational work while space complexity describes extra storage, and the two can trade against each other. dynamic programming decomposes a problem into overlapping subproblems and stores solved results to avoid repeated work. One layer deeper, a typical method defines a state, derives a recurrence, and evaluates states in dependency order or by memoized recursion. A useful distinction is that its key difference from ordinary divide-and-conquer is the repeated appearance of the same subproblems. This becomes concrete when edit distance, knapsack, and many sequence-optimization problems can be modeled this way. A common misunderstanding is that dynamic programming is not simply a two-dimensional array; choosing a sufficient but compact state is the real challenge The edge conditions still matter because If the state space itself is enormous, dynamic programming may still be impractical and require compression or another approach.

From a high-level view, a greedy algorithm makes the locally most attractive choice at each step in the hope that the choices form a global optimum. A fuller explanation is that correct greedy behavior usually depends on exchange properties, optimal substructure, or another proof rather than intuition. What should be separated here is that dynamic programming preserves multiple states while a greedy method usually commits to one direction and is often simpler and faster. In real tasks, this becomes tangible because interval scheduling, minimum spanning trees, and some coding problems admit provably correct greedy rules. The limiting conditions matter too: A correctness proof is as important as runtime efficiency when designing a greedy algorithm. One reason greedy algorithms is often misunderstood is that not every optimization problem is greedy-solvable because a local optimum can destroy a better future combination.

a hash table maps keys into a finite set of buckets and provides very fast average lookup and update. The underlying mechanism is that because the key space is larger than the bucket set, different keys inevitably collide. Its practical value is clear because caches, symbol tables, deduplication systems, and key-value indexes rely on fast hash-table access. One important contrast is that chaining stores colliding entries in an auxiliary structure while open addressing searches for another slot inside the table. A frequent mistake is to think that a good hash function can distribute keys more evenly but cannot mathematically eliminate all collisions This picture still depends on the fact that High load factors or adversarial inputs degrade performance, so implementations resize and rehash.

In real tasks, this becomes tangible because insurance pricing, quality control, and Monte Carlo simulation all rely on stable averages over many samples. The limiting conditions matter too: Strong dependence or heavy-tailed data can violate assumptions of simple forms of the theorem. One reason law of large numbers is often misunderstood is that a large sample does not make every observation close to the expectation because it is the aggregate average that stabilizes.

A fuller explanation is that surface processes break and transport rock into sediment, while heat and pressure underground alter minerals and can lead to remelting. What should be separated here is that the three major rock classes are distinguished by formation process rather than one fixed chemical composition. In real tasks, this becomes tangible because landform analysis, mineral resources, and reconstruction of Earth history all rely on the rock-cycle framework. The limiting conditions matter too: A complete cycle can take millions to hundreds of millions of years and cannot be observed directly from start to finish. One reason rock cycle is often misunderstood is that rocks do not remain unchanged forever because geological processes continually reshape them over long timescales.
